title: The Doire ghlas weaver's daughter sews by lantern
summary: At the fair's close on its first northern day, a Doire ghlas weaver's daughter left minding her mother's stall sews a second white thread into an unsold bolt after the buyers have gone. Asked why she troubles with it unwatched, she says the mark goes in whether anyone buys it or not, since a thread sewn only for show is no mark at all.

title: Baile chiar's weavers name their own thread pale
summary: Rather than claim An Snàthainn Geal already spoken for, the weavers of Baile chiar work a grey scarcely darker than the wool into the selvedge of their own finer bolts. An old weaver tells Daniel Frayne, who asks why the south troubles to copy a northern habit, that she has woven forty years without her name on a bolt and does not mean to die without it.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail begins the one sheet
summary: Catrìona nic Neacail, a Board surveyor sixteen years standing, begins drawing every stretch of the true vein still unopened onto a single leaf, working outward through the Board's own scattered rolls a shire at a time and riding to settle every ground the rolls disagree on.

title: A concession-holder asks the sheet a plain question
summary: A concession-holder of four generations' standing stands before the finished sheet the better part of an hour, then asks Catrìona nic Neacail plainly whether the red marked over his own family's ground means ten years or thirty, having daughters to settle and no wish to be told later that the Board had always known and never troubled to colour it in.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail named surveyor-general
summary: The Board names Catrìona nic Neacail surveyor-general, an office left empty three years for want of anyone troubling to ask what it was for, until her one-sheet map of the vein's last unworked stretches made plain that somebody ought to answer for the whole of what it showed. She is the youngest to hold it in living memory.

title: Ruairidh the cellar boy
summary: A clerk's boy of twelve who has fetched bundles in the Board's own cellar at Cathair mhòr for three years tells Catrìona nic Neacail she is the first to ask him to read a label aloud rather than simply hand a bundle across. He helps her keep the tally of the week's search among the old presses.

title: Two surveys read side by side
summary: Catrìona nic Neacail sits late at the Board's own table beneath her own sheet, reading her map and Iain Mapa's thirty-year-old survey side by side by lamplight, the same failing ground marked out in the same terms three decades apart, and cannot say which survey troubles her more, the one that found the truth or the one believed too late to matter.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail's visit to Muileann chiar
summary: Catrìona nic Neacail rides east to Muileann chiar and sits with Iain mac Ruairidh, three-and-sixty and failing, in what proves his last spring. He shows her his own copy of his old survey with the Board's receipt still pinned to it, and asks whether the school at Caol shean still keeps its old question about the vein.

title: Iain Mapa buried by Comann an Airgid
summary: Comann an Airgid of Muileann chiar, which had paid Iain mac Ruairidh's small pension ten years, buries him with an ounce of its own refined silver laid beside him, its master saying over him that he had gone into more of the mountain's dark than any three men living and had never once come up lying about what he found there.

title: Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill sends her husband's papers south
summary: Going through her husband's papers, Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill finds the folded survey with the Board's old receipt still pinned to it and sends the whole of it to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, writing only that he had asked more than once it not be lost a second time, and that she knew no safer place to send it.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail resigns the surveyor-general's office
summary: Within the year of finding Iain Mapa's old survey, Catrìona nic Neacail resigns as surveyor-general, the Board's own minute recording it in four flat lines, and asks a place teaching at Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean, judging the mountain's own answers now the only lesson in her trade worth the passing on.

title: Muileann dhearg's maor counts the empty houses
summary: Muileann dhearg's maor keeps a count of houses left empty as families leave for the ports and the southern yards, a tally kept at first from ordinary habit and then from something nearer alarm, running within three years to above sixty within the shire's own walls.

title: The Fèidh hall's last teacher locks its door
summary: The last teacher of Muileann dhearg's Fèidh hall, given back to Scoiltean nan Draoidhean not ten years before, locks its door herself for want of a congregation left to keep it and carries the key to the maor's own house rather than leave it with no one.

title: Ceann leathan raises Còmhrag Ceann leathan's gate-price
summary: With the harbour dues at Ceann leathan fallen by half as coal-ships wait for cargoes that come in half loaded, the fair-wardens, whose town lives as much off the coal trade as off the yearly melee, raise the gate-price of Còmhrag Ceann leathan to make up what the quay no longer earns.

title: The Muileann dhearg bell rings Catrìona's first lecture
summary: Catrìona nic Neacail gives her first lecture at Caol shean in the same wood where Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain once first put the old question to her students, and the bell taken down from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, hung now in the school's own tower, is rung for the first time to call the school in.

title: The grey twill first on the pole
summary: Daniel Frayne, six months in Tional nan Tuathach's chair, watches the first cloth of the fair's northern day go up on its pole at Muileann òg: a grey twill of Doire ghlas dyed with the shire's own bark, with a single white thread at the selvedge.

title: Duilleag na Fèithe hung on the chamber wall
summary: Catrìona nic Neacail publishes Duilleag na Fèithe in an Dùbhlachd in the plainest way the Board knows, hanging it on the wall of its own chamber at Cathair mhòr, where every surveyor, clerk and concession-holder who comes can stand before it.

title: Iain Mapa dies at his workbench
summary: Iain mac Ruairidh dies at his own workbench at Muileann chiar in the first days of an Cèitean, not a fortnight after Catrìona nic Neacail's visit; Mòr finds him in the evening with small objects laid out before him in an order only he had understood.
